title: Ambient concrete carbonation is a trivial contributor in mitigating carbon dioxide emissions from cement production
abstract: Abstract Ambient carbonation—the passive uptake of atmospheric carbon dioxide into the alkaline pore solution of concrete—has been proposed to mitigate carbon dioxide emissions from cement production. Herein, we apply thermodynamic and diffusion-based analyses within a Monte Carlo framework to evaluate the extent and rate of ambient carbonation across concrete formulations and geometries (i.e., described by their surface-to-volume ratio, ranging between 0.01-to-80, /m), globally. The analysis indicates that, by 2030, the carbonation of concrete placed in service, globally, under ambient conditions, is projected to uptake around 0.23 gigatonnes annually (i.e., <10% of annual cement clinker emissions). Thus, the amount of carbon dioxide sequestered by ambient carbonation is negligible compared to the quantities emitted during cement production. Importantly, this analysis underscores the importance of prioritizing near-term industrial decarbonization and of advancing intentional climate change mitigation solutions that deliver meaningful and timely reductions in anthropogenic carbon dioxide emissions.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Concrete carbonates passively under ambient conditions (“ambient carbonation”) whereby carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) in the atmosphere (~420 ppm, ~0.042 vol. % CO 2 ) is absorbed into the concrete’s alkaline pore solution. This absorbed CO 2  reacts with compounds, including calcium hydroxide, calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H) and other alkaline minerals via so-called “carbonation” reactions. These reactions, which ultimately lead to the formation of calcium carbonate (CaCO 3 ) and poorly-crystalline silicate- and aluminate phases, are accompanied by the reduction in the pH of the concrete’s alkaline pore solution, and the carbonation-induced decomposition (i.e., consumption or decalcification) of the concrete’s native hydration products (e.g., portlandite: Ca(OH) 2  and calcium silicate hydrate: C-S-H). While ambient carbonation is well-known to detrimentally affect the durability and service life of reinforced and unreinforced concrete structures (e.g., due to the onset of steel corrosion 1 , 2  and carbonation shrinkage 3 , 4 ), recent studies have suggested that ambient carbonation may, in fact, be beneficial—by making use of the built environment as a CO 2  sink—and thus, could mitigate the significant CO 2  emissions resulting from Ordinary Portland Cement (OPC) clinker production 5 , 6 .

Concrete is the most widely produced synthetic material globally, with an annual production of ~30 billion tonnes 6 , 7 . But, on account of the carbon-intensive nature of the production process, cement (“OPC”)—the glue in concrete—is responsible for ~10% of global CO 2  emissions 6 , 7 . For context, on average, ~1 tonne of CO 2  is emitted per tonne of OPC’s clinker produced, which explains OPC’s substantial embodied Carbon Intensity (eCI). The majority of such CO 2  emissions are associated with clinker production, with only 10% of the emissions resulting from transport 8 ,  9 ,  10 – 11 . Recent discourse suggests that the ambient carbonation of concrete is a means for mitigating OPC production’s CO 2  emissions. While the provenance of this mitigation benefit is unclear, the calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) formed during ambient carbonation of concrete is unquestionably a durable CO₂ sink—stable at ambient pressure and temperature over geological timescales 12 ,  13 – 14 . The ambient carbonation of concrete depends on multiple factors including: the exposed surface area-to-volume ratio of the concrete (s/v, m −1 ), the environmental conditions, namely, temperature (T, °C), relative humidity (RH, %), pressure (p, atm), and CO 2  concentration (vol. %) in the atmosphere ([CO 2 ]); and the chemical composition of the concrete’s cementitious binder—in particular its alkali/alkaline element content 10 , 15 ,  16 ,  17 ,  18 – 19 .

Ambient carbonation has been suggested to abate between 10 and 50 mass % of the CO 2  emissions associated with clinker production 5 , 10 , 20 ,  21 – 22 . Several studies have estimated that increasing concrete construction could reduce global CO 2  emissions—and, by extension, atmospheric CO 2  accumulations—through ambient carbonation. While ambient carbonation is well known to detrimentally affect the durability of concrete structures—e.g., by promoting steel reinforcement corrosion and carbonation shrinkage 1 , 23 , 24 —its potential to serve as an  intentional, viable and beneficial  technological pathway for CO₂ mitigation remains far less certain 9 , 10 , 18 . Therefore, this study critically examines whether ambient carbonation is indeed a meaningful approach for reducing the eCI of cement production. We estimate the median, upper, and lower bounds for CO 2  absorption (considering reaction and transport) in concrete. The analysis, albeit simplified, accounts for the key variables—including the concrete’s mixture design, the OPC content and degree of hydration, accessible porosity, and the  s/v  of concrete elements—to estimate the extent of CO 2  uptake. A representative structural service life of 50 years 25 , 26  is assumed in this analysis, although it is acknowledged that actual service life may vary, with structures being in use for both shorter and significantly longer periods of time.

sections.heading: Carbonation potential
paragraphs: Thermodynamic modeling was used to estimate the carbonation potential of a cementitious binder as a function of its degree of hydration (DoH) and water-to-cement  (w/c)  ratio. The phase assemblage of a carbonated “neat OPC” hydrated to 85% DoH is presented in Fig.  1a 27 ,  28 ,  29 – 30 . Prior to carbonation, the OPC hydration products are portlandite (Ca(OH) 2 ), ettringite, calcium silicate hydrates (C-S-H), and monosulfoaluminate 30 , 31 . As CO 2  is introduced into the system, the calcium in the hydration products is progressively converted into CaCO 3 , while the silicon and aluminum species are released and subsequently reprecipitate as silica- and alumina-rich compounds 32 . Complete carbonation is observed for a pore solution pH of 9.6 (i.e., higher than the 1% phenolphthalein test, which suggests a pH <8.6 33 , 34 ) as has been observed elsewhere 34 , 35 . At this pH level, quantitative phase analysis confirms that all calcium-bearing phases within the carbonated region are fully carbonated—leaving no residual portlandite or C-S-H detectable 33 , 36 . Figure  1b  shows the influence of  w/ c  and the degree of hydration (DoH) on the maximum quantity of CO 2  absorbed by a hydrated type I/II OPC during carbonation. Herein, carbonation refers to the reaction of hydrated OPC compounds (e.g., portlandite and AFm phases), excluding anhydrous phases, such as alite and belite. The carbonation of these anhydrous phases proceeds via a dissolution–precipitation mechanism that first requires the formation of the hydration products (e.g., C–S–H, portlandite, and AFm phases), which subsequently carbonate 32 . The evolution of the pore solution pH following carbonation, the porosity, and the maximum CO 2  uptake (i.e., “CO 2 absorb”) of the concrete were calculated and used as inputs in the Monte Carlo simulations for carbonation modeling. Fig. 1 Carbonation modeling of concrete. a  Thermodynamic modeling of the phase assemblage evolution of a hydrated OPC for  w/c  = 0.40, and DoH = 85% following increasing CO 2  exposure. Also shown is the evolution of the pore solution pH. Mineral phase abbreviations: Aq. phase: pore solution, CH: portlandite, Ms: calcium monosulfoaluminate, Mc: calcium monocarboaluminate, Ett: ettringite, CSH: C-S-H, Gyp: gypsum, SiO 2 : amorphous silica, CaCO 3 : calcite, C3FS0.84H: Al-Fe siliceous hydrogarnet.  b  The maximum quantity of CO2 that can react with a liter of hydrated OPC (mol/LOPC) as a function of the  w/c  and degree of (OPC) hydration.  c  A comparison between the measured and calculated (using Eq.  4 ) carbonation depths wherein the measurements are data sourced from the literature 61 ,  62 ,  63 ,  64 ,  65 – 66 . The normalized root mean square error (nRMSE) indicates that the predicted carbonation depth is aligned with experimental data. Also, shown are the +/−20% prediction estimates.  d  Long-term ambient carbonation depths up to 50 years taken from the literature with a comparison to the median, lower and upper bound estimates calculated using Eq.  4 46 , 65 , 144 ,  145 ,  146 ,  147 ,  148 – 149 . The upper and lower bound estimates represent the range of carbonation depths under the most and least favorable conditions. At 50 years, the upper and lower bound depth of carbonation estimates ( xc ) are 38.2 mm and 3.6 mm, respectively, with a median of 13.8 mm. Also shown is the effect of surface-to-volume ratio ( s/v ) on:  e  the number of years required to achieve 1%, 10%, 50% and 90% carbonation for a representative concrete formulation [14 mass % OPC,  w/c  = 0.45,  a/b  = 5.5, DoH = 85%], and  f  the percentage of OPC’s production emissions abated in the first year of service for a representative concrete section.

sections.heading: Carbonation modeling
paragraphs: The depth of carbonation calculated using Eqs.  4 and  5  (see “Methods”) was compared against literature data for binders consisting of OPC and supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) (see Fig.  1c ). Here, the effective diffusion coefficient of the concrete was estimated using Eq.  6  (see “Methods”) and used to calculate the depth of carbonation using Eq.  5 . Analysis of Eq.  6  shows that there are two domains that most affect the values of the constants  α  and  β  (fitting constants) as related to the aggregate to binder ratio ( a/b ), where, (i)  a/b  < 3, and  α  = 4.1 × 10 −5  cm 2 /s and  β  = 1, and (ii)  a/b  > 3,  α  = 2.5 × 10 −7  cm 2 /s and  β  = 0.1. The predictions of the ambient carbonation model were tested against long-term literature data (i.e., up to 50 years; see Fig.  1d ) to determine whether the predicted values encompassed the upper, lower, and median estimates of carbonation depth. An unbiased sensitivity analysis using the Monte Carlo method was used to assess how the carbonation depth changed in relation to the influential variables noted in Eq.  5 . In general, Eq.  5 ’s median estimate reasonably described experimental data of the measured carbonation depth.

A model concrete composed of 14 mass % OPC,  w/c  = 0.45,  a/b  = 5.5, DoH = 85% was used to test the carbonation estimates. Of particular interest is to understand how the macroscopic  s/v  affects the time required for carbonation, i.e., to achieve different degrees of carbonation, and counteract the emissions associated with OPC production. It should be noted that this analysis considers a pristine/uncracked concrete. Since concrete is known to (always) feature cracks, the effect of cracks, big-and-small, is to increase the  s/v  (although how much so, is quantitatively unclear because of carbonation in-filling of cracks and pores 37 ,  38 – 39 ), such that carbonation occurs faster for a cracked as opposed to an uncracked material [N.B.: in the limit, i.e., after “infinite” time, the extent of CO 2  absorption by a cracked and uncracked material would be equivalent]. For pristine concrete, a conservative case, kinetically speaking, Fig.  1e  shows the time required to achieve different extents of carbonation of concrete under ambient conditions across a variety of  s/v . For example, an uncracked structural concrete element, e.g., a concrete beam, pavement or concrete slab, with  s/v  = 10 m −1  whose faces are fully exposed to the atmosphere, would require up to 1000 years to achieve 50% carbonation under ambient conditions. A concrete element with  s/v  of 80 m −1  similar to a concrete masonry unit (CMU), would require ~14 years to achieve 50% carbonation, although the actual carbonation kinetics could be significantly faster due to its porous texture. This simple analysis indicates that under ambient conditions, typical concrete elements would need enormously long reaction times (>50 years) to even partially reabsorb the CO 2  emissions resulting from their constituent OPC’s production 40 ,  41 ,  42 ,  43 – 44 . However, claims of effectively carbonating recycled concrete aggregates (RCAs) are less controversial, e.g., since the model indicates that only ~1 year is required to fully carbonate a fully exposed RCA fine aggregate ( d p  [particle diameter] <9.5 mm,  s/v  ~ 630 m −1 ) 45  under ambient exposure conditions. Following similar analysis, Fig.  1f  shows the impact of  s/v  on ambient carbonation, wherein it is seen that less than <2 mass % of OPC’s production emissions are abated during the first year in service for the quantity of OPC contained in a typical concrete element with  s/v  ~ 10 m −1 , indicating both the very slow nature of ambient carbonation, and its ability to only negligibly counteract OPC’s production emissions.

sections.heading: Carbonation behavior at ambient CO 2  conditions (“passive carbonation”)
paragraphs: The effects of water-to-binder mass ratio ( w/b ), OPC’s degree of hydration, aggregate-to-binder ratio ( a/b) , and  s/v  on concrete’s carbonation over 50 years under ambient conditions are shown in Fig.  2a–h . The carbonation model indicates that a greater penetration depth results for lower degrees of hydration (Fig.  2a ). This trend is explained by the fact that increasing hydration reduces the porosity of the concrete, thus reducing gas diffusion 36 , 46 ,  47 – 48 . Although greater levels of C-S-H, Ca(OH) 2  are available in higher DoH systems, the restriction in gas transport hinders CO 2  uptake. The model predicts a monotonous increase in penetration (carbonation) depth with increasing  w/c  as shown in Fig.  2c, d , respectively. This is because the porosity increases with  w/c , thus improving gas transport. An increasing aggregate-to-binder ratio causes a direct increase in CO 2  uptake due to increased transport with a decreasing binder content. Unsurprisingly, the 1-D carbonation depth is not affected by the  s/v  (see also Eqs.  4 and  5 , wherein the diffusion coefficient is independent of  s/v ), as shown in Fig.  2g . However, a much smaller volume of the section has carbonated, for materials with a smaller  s/v 32 . A clear limitation of the modeling approach is that it does not consider pore (moisture) saturation levels, which can substantially affect carbonation rates. The dependence of carbonation on pore saturation is inherently non-monotonic: while decreasing saturation (i.e., reduced water content) enhances gas transport and can accelerate carbonation, excessively low saturation limits the availability of pore solution required for CO₂ dissolution and subsequent reaction, thereby reducing carbonation rates 46 , 47 , 49 . Conversely, high saturation restricts CO₂ diffusivity and suppresses carbonation. As a result, carbonation rates are generally maximized at intermediate saturation levels, typically corresponding to relative humidity (RH) values of ~70%. In this context, the adoption of RH ≈ 70% serves two purposes. First, it is broadly consistent with average ambient conditions across inhabited regions globally 50 ,  51 – 52 . Second, and more importantly, it corresponds to near-optimal conditions for carbonation, thereby providing a reasonable upper-bound estimate of carbonation potential under passive exposure scenarios 46 , 47 , 49 . We acknowledge that RH effects depend enormously on prevailing weather (T, RH) conditions, and the exposure of the concrete (wet, dry, intermittent, above-ground, painted, occluded or not, etc). These effects are very complicated to assess, even parametrically, and thus were not considered in this analysis. Furthermore, these kinetic effects of pore saturation are more important for accelerated (enforced, non-passive) carbonation, wherein carbonation is effected over shorter time periods, albeit at much higher CO 2  concentrations. Fig. 2 Carbonation behavior of concrete at ambient CO 2  conditions. The carbonation depth and extent of CO 2  uptake in mature (50-year-old) concrete as a function of:  a ,  b  the cement’s degree of hydration;  c ,  d  the water-to-binder mass ratio;  e ,  f  the aggregate-to binder mass ratio; and  g ,  h  the surface area-to-volume ratio of the element. The gradient data points were generated using Monte Carlo simulations, incorporating the probabilistic distributions of each variable. The impact of SCM content on:  i  penetration depth, and CO 2  uptake for  j s/v  = 10 m −1 , k  s/v  = 50 m −1  and  l s/v  = 100 m −1 . This is a representative concrete formulation with: 14 mass % OPC (binder, b),  w/b  = 0.45,  a/b  = 5.5, DoH OPC  = 85%, DoH SCM  = 40%.

sections.heading: Impact of SCMs
paragraphs: The carbonation of blended binders was additionally evaluated to highlight the impact of SCMs on CO 2  uptake. A high Ca-content, mid Ca-content and low Ca-content SCM were considered as OPC replacement materials to represent blast furnace slag (BFS), Class C fly ash and Class F fly ash, respectively. These SCMs are widely used, and their OPC replacement levels can range from 0 to 95 mass % (OPC replacement) depending on prevailing standards 53 ,  54 ,  55 – 56 . Here, the SCMs have all reacted 40% after 28 days of aging 57 ,  58 ,  59 – 60 —a conservative estimate for more prolonged periods of aging. Three representative concrete elements with  w/c  = 0.45,  a/b  = 5.5 and three different values of  s/v  (10, 50, and 100 m −1 ) were examined to highlight the impact of SCM replacement after 50 years of ambient carbonation. Figure  2i  shows the evolution of the (carbonation) penetration depth as a function of increasing SCM replacement, which is affected by opposing mechanisms: (i) alkalinity depletion—pozzolanic reactions consume portlandite, lowering the buffering capacity of the pore solution and accelerating carbonation, (ii) dilution effect—clinker replacement reduces the overall CaO content of the binder, diminishing the alkaline reserve available to absorb (neutralize) CO 2 , and (iii) transport property alterations—SCMs refine the pore structure and reduce the diffusivity of CO 2  and moisture, thereby slowing ingress. The net carbonation depth reflects the balance among these mechanisms, with alkalinity depletion and dilution typically outweighing transport reductions (microstructure densification) at typical SCM replacement levels, particularly after long time scales 61 ,  62 ,  63 ,  64 ,  65 – 66 . After 50 years of ambient carbonation, the penetration depth increased from 13.25 mm in the control (neat OPC concrete) to 22.4, 24.3, and 26.0 mm with increasing substitution of SCMs, corresponding to the dominant effect of alkali dilution and depletion by SCMs. As expected, the amount of CO 2  uptake per unit mass of binder is highly dependent on the macroscopic surface-to-volume ratio ( s/v ), as illustrated in Fig.  2j–l .

The influence of SCMs on CO 2  uptake operates through two competing mechanisms: (1) enhanced CO₂ penetration due to the inclusion of SCMs, which increases the volume of concrete that has carbonated especially after long time scales; and (2) a reduction in the carbonation potential (mass) per unit volume, owing to the dilution of OPC (i.e., reduction in the Ca-content) by SCMs. For a low  s/v  of 10 m −1 , the deeper carbonation induced by the SCM dominates, resulting in an increase in CO 2  uptake compared to the neat OPC baseline (0.054 kg CO 2 /kg cement ): 0.069 kg CO 2 /kg cement  for BFS, 0.066 kg CO 2 /kg cement  for Class C fly ash, and 0.065 kg CO 2 /kg cement  for Class F fly ash (Fig.  2j ). At a moderate  s/v  of 50 m −1 , CO 2  uptake initially increases with SCM content but eventually declines beyond a certain threshold (Fig.  2k ), indicating a shift in control from carbonation depth to the lower intrinsic carbonation capacity of SCM-blended binders. At a high  s/v  of 100 m −1 —where the concrete is expected to carbonate fully—the CO 2  uptake aligns with the thermodynamic (compositional) carbonation potential, decreasing from 0.41 kg CO 2 /kg cement in neat OPC to 0.29, 0.27, and 0.25 kg CO 2 /kg cement for slag, Class C, and Class F binders, respectively (Fig.  3l ). Fig. 3 Global cement production and CO 2  emissions. a  The annual production of cement by global regions from 1930 to 2030 (USA, China, Europe (EU), and the Rest of World (ROW)) 69 ,  70 – 71 .  b  The extent of annual cement production with individual contributions of process and fossil fuel related CO 2  emissions 72 , 73 , and  c  the quantity of global cumulative cement production and associated CO 2  emissions from process and fossil fuel sources from 1930 to 2030.

sections.heading: Global cement production and CO₂ emissions
paragraphs: Clinker manufacture requires the calcination of the raw materials (e.g., limestone, shale, clay, etc.) in a rotary kiln up to 1450 °C to form the clinker minerals. Depending on the clinker manufacturing process, energy use can range from 3 to 6 GJ/t clinker . Furthermore, the fuel type dictates the fossil fuel emissions factor associated with clinker production, such that it can range from 0.08 to 0.60 kg CO 2 /kg clinker , with the lowest factors realized using renewable energy and the upper bound based on coal sources. A summary of the annual and cumulative global cement production 72 , 73 , process emissions 72  and fossil fuel emissions 73  are shown in Fig.  3b, c . From 1930 to 2022, cement production and associated emissions have risen sharply, reflecting the exponential growth in global cement demand driven by industrialization and urbanization. The 2022 global process and fossil fuel CO 2  emissions factors (kg CO 2 /kg cement ) were applied to the 2030 estimate of cement production to ascertain future contributions of process and fuel emissions. Of course, the life cycle eCI of concrete is impacted by other factors, such as mixing and curing operations, transportation, and the use of metal reinforcement. These factors are, however, extrinsic to concrete as a material, and therefore, only the process and fossil fuel emissions are considered in this analysis.

sections.heading: CO₂ uptake of the global concrete inventory
paragraphs: The results of the Monte Carlo simulations for the time-dependent cumulative CO 2  uptake per unit mass of binder are shown in Fig.  4a–c , for China, USA and ROW/Europe. Here, a representative average service life of 50 years is assumed for global concrete structures, within a practical range of 35–75 years 5 , 17 . For each service year (0–50 years), the median CO 2  uptake across all Monte Carlo simulations is ascertained to describe typical carbonation behavior over time. The median cumulative CO 2  uptake after 50 years for each region is as follows: (a) China = 0.070 kg CO 2 /kg cement , (b) Europe/ROW = 0.066 kg CO 2 /kg cement , and (c) USA = 0.090 kg CO 2 /kg cement . The higher estimate of CO 2  uptake in the U.S. is due to the higher proportions of lower-strength concrete (i.e., ≤C15 and C16–C23) as compared to China and Europe (see Table  2 ). Figure  4d  presents the binder’s annual CO 2  uptake rate for each region, i.e., the first (time) derivative with respect to the cumulative binder CO 2  uptake. This derivative reflects the rate of carbonation-induced CO 2  absorption as a function of time, thereby illustrating how the uptake kinetics evolve over the service life of concrete. In all regions, the CO 2  uptake rate is highest during the early years of exposure, corresponding to the rapid carbonation of near-surface layers, and progressively declines as the carbonation front advances and diffusion resistance increases. Fig. 4 CO 2  uptake kinetics over the service life of concrete. Representative Monte Carlo simulation results showing the 50-year median value of cumulative CO 2  uptake by the concrete’s binder (kgCO 2 /kg binder ) via ambient carbonation across 100,000 sampling points for:  a  China,  b  Europe or ROW, and  c  USA. The Monte Carlo simulation estimates incorporate probability distributions of each variable.  d  Annual binder CO 2  uptake rate (kgCO 2 /kg binder /year) for each region, described as the first-derivative with respect to time of the cumulative binder CO 2  uptake (kgCO 2 /kg binder ).

The global in-service concrete stock constitutes an unambiguous sink for atmospheric CO 2  via ongoing ambient carbonation. This uptake continues as concrete produced and emplaced in the preceding years continues to carbonate; with more recently placed concrete incrementing such uptake. In principle, the enormous in-service concrete stock could be envisioned as a significant CO 2  reservoir—potentially capable of offsetting emissions from past, present, and future cement production, thereby reducing the reliance on additional mitigation measures. However, our analysis categorically indicates otherwise. Figure  5a  presents estimates of the annual CO₂ uptake by the global in-service concrete stock placed from 1930 to 2030. By 2030, this annual absorption is expected to result in the uptake of ~0.23 GtCO 2 , contributing to the abatement of approximately ~12.7% and ~7.6% of process and total emissions (see Fig.  5b ), respectively. This estimate lies at the lower end of previous estimates, which suggest a range between 11-to-57% abatement of process emissions 5 , 10 , 74 ,  75 ,  76 – 77 . It should be noted that, as shown in (and inferred via) Fig.  1e, f , increasing the surface area to volume ratio can rapidly increase the carbonation rate. However, one can only guess what the “true”  s/v  of concrete is as it carbonates in its ambient environment? Importantly, it must be noted that the approach applied herein does not account for secondary-life, e.g., the extended exposure of construction and demolition waste (C&DW), where further CO 2  absorption could occur 5 , 20 , 76 , 78 . Said differently, although concrete has the potential to significantly reabsorb CO 2  through carbonation during its secondary life, the actual extent of this uptake is expected to be limited under typical conditions 17 , 79 , 80 . While crushing increases the surface area of recycled concrete, studies have shown that CO 2  diffusion within stockpiled demolished concrete is slow 79 , 80 . Furthermore, compaction from rainfall and short storage times before reuse further reduces the degree of carbonation achieved during storage 79 . Moreover, most demolished concrete is either landfilled or repurposed in low-exposure applications (e.g., as road base), where contact with atmospheric CO 2  is limited and carbonation proceeds slowly due to restricted air exposure 81 ,  82 – 83 . Of course, there remains considerable further uncertainty regarding the progress of carbonation as a function of the exposure conditions: e.g., whether the concrete is sheltered, inside a structure, covered by a facade, covered with mortar, or a mortar component itself—i.e., beyond materials characteristics including  w/c , compressive strength, porosity, etc 5 , 77 . These factors expectedly would affect the carbonation depth and CO 2  uptake as estimated by the modeling approach shown in Fig.  2a–l . Fig. 5 CO 2  uptake of the global concrete inventory. a  An estimate of annual CO 2  uptake by the global concrete stock (USA, EU, China, Rest of World). Here, uptake reflects ongoing carbonation, each year, of the existing in-service concrete. For example, in a given year (e.g., at the end of 2030), concrete produced in 2029 contributes only 2 years of carbonation (2029, 2030), while older concretes experience longer periods of carbonation.  b  Annual percentage abatement of CO 2  emissions by concrete’s carbonation, expressed relative to process emissions and total emissions from clinker production.  c  Annual CO 2  emissions from cement production, contextualized against the annual CO 2  absorption of in-service concrete, and the net impact on annual emissions.  d  Cumulative CO 2  emissions from cement production, contextualized against the cumulative CO 2  uptake of in-service concrete, showing the net cumulative global CO 2  emissions from 1930 to 2030.

As of 1986, Europe produced the most cement clinker (and concrete), thereby presenting the largest ambient carbonation sink. After this time, the ROW (i.e., largely due to India; not including China) started to produce more cement than Europe. Post-1993, China began to produce more cement than Europe, and after 2001, produced more than the ROW 69 ,  70 – 71 . On a regional basis, China and the ROW were therefore estimated to absorb the largest fractions of CO 2  annually by 2022; i.e., 0.094 GtCO 2  and 0.065 GtCO 2 , respectively, in line with their fraction of cement clinker production since the 1990’s. The cement industry seeks to reduce cement-related CO 2  emissions by 40% by 2030 10 , 18 , 19 . As noted above, the amount of ambient CO 2  absorption by the “in service” concrete inventory contributes  trivially  towards fulfilling this target as shown in Fig.  5b, c  where the average CO 2  absorption by carbonation reduces the CO 2  emissions resulting from cement production by <10% at best. For example, over the full period from 1930 to 2030, as seen in Fig.  5d  it is clear that the vast majority of CO 2  released from cement clinker production remains unmitigated, leading to an unambiguous, persistent and ever-growing accumulation of CO 2  in the atmosphere. The Global Carbon Project (GCP) states that to avoid the 1.5 (or 2 °C) temperature increase threshold by 2050, globally we can emit only ~380 (or ~1230) GtCO 2  by 2050, respectively 72 , 73 . Against this framing, relying on ambient carbonation to significantly reduce ongoing CO 2  emissions from cement production in any meaningful way is unrealistic, as cement production alone is expected to contribute ~2.6 to 2.8 GtCO 2  (net emissions) annually from 2020 to 2030. If the ~2.8 GtCO 2  emissions level per year rate remains constant until 2050, cement production alone would cumulatively contribute approximately ~85 GtCO 2 , accounting for ~23% of the remaining carbon budget implied by the 1.5 °C threshold. This highlights that ambient carbonation is by no means able to mitigate, in any substantial way, the climate impact of cement production.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: This study estimates the potential of the ambient carbonation of concrete to act as a global atmospheric CO 2  sink. The analysis indicates that annual CO 2  uptake by the global concrete inventory over its service life is substantially lower than the annual emissions from cement clinker production, resulting in an ever-increasing CO 2  burden. This imbalance arises because the rate of CO₂ emissions greatly exceeds the rate and extent of CO 2  uptake through ambient carbonation. By 2030, carbonation of the in-service concrete stock under ambient conditions is projected to absorb ~0.23 GtCO 2  per year, equivalent to <10% of annual cement emissions. While this work clearly demonstrates that ambient carbonation is a CO 2  sink [N.B.: 230 million tonnes of CO 2  absorption in a year is by no means insignificant!], the projected uptake is at best, a small number vis-à-vis the cement industry’s: (a) projected CO 2  emissions in 2030 [~3.04 GtCO 2 ], and (b) the cement industry’s 2030 target of reducing cement’s annual emissions by 40% (i.e., a reduction of ~1.22 GtCO 2  which so far, appears physically and economically unrealizable). Thus, unambiguously, other more direct and impactful measures are required to achieve cement decarbonization via process transformations, accelerated carbonation, carbon capture and storage (CCS), and/or (atmospheric) carbon dioxide removal (CDR). Why? Relying on the ambient passive carbonation of concrete is simply not going to provide sufficient CO 2  absorption required to reduce cement’s CO 2  emissions in any substantial way.

sections.heading: Perspective
paragraphs: The production of cement clinker is the largest contributor to global industrial emissions 11 , 72 , 84 . While cement clinker production has continued to become increasingly energy efficient, process emissions from cement production continue to be notoriously difficult to abate. The cement industry continues to make steady, albeit slow progress to abate such emissions via multiple established, and emerging approaches including: cement use reductions (i.e., improving material use efficiencies), material substitution (clinker factor reductions, e.g., via the use of SCMs), the use of alternative fuels, waste heat recovery, carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) solutions, and new process technologies (e.g., the ZeroCAL process which eliminates process CO 2  emissions) 85 ,  86 ,  87 ,  88 ,  89 ,  90 ,  91 ,  92 ,  93 – 94 . While passive carbonation of the in-service concrete inventory has been extensively suggested to serve as a substantial contributor to clinker emissions reductions (i.e., via passive, or ambient carbonation) 5 , 10 , 20 ,  21 – 22 , 74 , 84 , 95 ,  96 – 97 —the analysis presented herein clearly indicates otherwise. Much of the optimism regarding passive carbonation arises from perhaps overly favorable assumptions about the fate of end-of-life concrete, wherein size reductions during demolition are expected to accelerate passive carbonation rates. However, these assumptions neglect existing practices of waste management, generally speaking. In most places, demolished concrete is deposited in landfills, accumulated in stockpiles or re-used as an aggregate. These are environments where passive gas transport is restricted, and only a limited fraction of material is accessible to air. Under such conditions, the role of post-demolition carbonation in mitigating CO₂ emissions is expected to be highly limited. This may change, however, if pulverized concrete residuals (e.g., prior to recycling as aggregate) were to be exposed to accelerated carbonation at the end of life; in which case, it is conceivable that end-of-life carbonation could be more substantial than in-service life carbonation. But, excluding this practice, which is uncommon today, our analysis therefore adopts a more conservative stance relevant to passive carbonation recognizing both the practical constraints of end-of-life carbonation and the fact that no existing models fully capture its complexities. Meanwhile, substantial ongoing and retrospective uncertainty (e.g., of concrete composition, cement content, and composition, in service  s/v , T, RH conditions, etc.) persists in precisely defining the influential variables that affect passive CO 2  uptake. For these reasons, it is necessary that ongoing and amplifying advocacy of passive carbonation as a CO 2  mitigation strategy for the cement industry moderate immediately.

While there is no question that the built environment serves as a substantial passive carbon sink, it is far more likely that approaches based on accelerated carbonation (carbon dioxide utilization) of precast concrete products and/or demolished concrete materials (prior to recycling or landfilling) 98 ,  99 – 100  or based on the incorporation of carbonate mineralized SCMs 101 , 102  or aggregates 103 , 104  and/or biochar 105 , 106  (albeit in small quantities, due to the strength reduction that results 106 ) may be more impactful. That said, the implementation of these conceivably more impactful methods needs to be accompanied by systemic changes in construction practices, standards, and policy incentives—to promote structural design optimization, improvement of material use efficiencies (i.e., reducing cement use via improved mixture proportioning, and SCM use) 107 , 108  and extending service life, and end-of-life recycling—to enhance material circularity, and thus reduce lifecycle carbon impact.

Unquestionably, what is important in each of these cases is to consider the net present value (NPV) of emissions reduction since CO 2  emissions reduced or eliminated today are most significant in terms of not breaching the residual carbon budget and thus limiting the extent of global warming that results 84 , 95 , 109 . Moreover, emissions mitigated today represent emissions that need not be removed or otherwise abated tomorrow. What this means is that the most impactful pathways of cement decarbonization are those that reduce, eliminate or abate emissions, near instantaneously temporally, and that do not  smear  emissions mitigation benefits over a long period of time in the manner of passive concrete carbonation.

sections.heading: Methods
paragraphs: The rate of concrete carbonation is a function of the concrete’s porosity, which controls the diffusion of CO 2  through the pore network as well as its strength. To establish a practical proxy for porosity, the distribution of concretes produced across strength classes was estimated (see Table  2 ) 20 , 78 . The knowledge of a concrete’s strength enables an indirect, albeit coarse, estimation of the concrete’s mixture proportions—by inference-based on empirical guidelines for input variables including: the water-to-cement ratio  (w/c)  and the aggregate-to-binder ratio  (a/b)  for different concrete grades (see Table  3 ) 140 ,  141 – 142 . These relationships allow regional concrete inventories to be parameterized in terms of their effective transport properties and carbonation potential, which form the key input variables for the Monte Carlo simulations of CO 2  uptake. It should be noted that the data from European regions are used to estimate the Rest of World (ROW) strength categories, as the ROW data are not readily available. Concretes with higher  w/c  and  a/b  ratios, which correspond to lower strength grades, exhibit greater carbonation susceptibility due to their more porous microstructure and lower binder content per unit volume. In contrast, higher-strength concretes proportioned with lower  w/c  and  a/b  ratios generally develop denser matrices that limit CO 2  ingress and reduce carbonation penetration.

A Monte Carlo simulation approach was used to assess the effective diffusion coefficient (Eq.  6 ), and in turn, the depth of carbonation (Eq.  5 ) during ambient atmospheric exposure (p CO2  ~ 0.04 vol. %, ~420 ppm). It should be noted that although global CO 2  concentrations have risen from 320 ppm to >420 ppm over the last century, for simplicity, 420 ppm was used throughout as a conservative estimate. In general, across all simulations, the ambient relative humidity was fixed at 70% (i.e., a level near the global average and that is favorable for concrete’s carbonation) 50 ,  51 – 52 , and the average temperature (T) was assumed to lie in the range of 20–30 °C 143 . It should be noted that most of the literature data compiled in this study (Fig.  1c, d ) are derived from long-term ambient carbonation exposure, typically under average conditions in the range of 20–30  °C 46 , 65 , 144 ,  145 ,  146 ,  147 ,  148 – 149 . As such, the adopted temperature range reflects common service environments rather than controlled or extreme conditions, with the understanding that higher and lower temperatures can meaningfully affect reaction rates (e.g., the activation energy of the carbonation reaction is ~16.8–20.6 kJ/mole, suggesting a modest dependence of temperature on carbonation reaction rates) 150 . While temperature influences carbonation through its effects on reaction kinetics and CO 2  solubility, its variability is implicitly embedded within the compiled dataset. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that temperature effects are also coupled with RH and moisture transport processes and are not fully captured by a single representative value. Therefore, similar to RH, the present approach should be interpreted as reflecting typical ambient carbonation behavior, rather than a fully resolved treatment of temperature-dependent mechanisms. The Monte Carlo simulations were carried out while varying the variables in Eq.  6  using a defined probability distribution (i.e., uniform or normal), and over a specified range for each variable. The total number of simulations carried out was 100,000 for each geographical region (Table  2 ). Here, the fraction of concrete within a given strength grade determined the number of simulations carried out, such that, e.g., for China: ( C  < 15) = 0.149 × 100,000; (C16–23) = 0.125 × 100,000; etc.: Exposure duration ( t , 0–50, years): a uniform distribution was used ( µ  = 25 years [mean],  σ  = 14.43 years [standard deviation]). An expected service life of 50 years was assumed as a central value for service life estimates of concretes ranging between 35 and 75 years 5 , 17 , 151 . Since precise distribution data of the service life of concrete structures is not available, we assume a uniform distribution. [Macroscopic]  s/v  (0.01–80 m −1 ): a uniform distribution was used ( µ  = 40 m −1 ,  σ  = 23.09 m −1 ). For example, large elements or submerged (or below-ground) or covered concrete are estimated to have  s/v  = 0.01 m −1 . For a standard structural element, such as a concrete beam, concrete column, pavement, or concrete slab,  s/v  ~ 10 m −1 . It is important to note that these estimates assume an uncracked surface, where CO 2  ingress occurs primarily through the micropores. In the case of dry-cast concrete with visible porous textures—such as concrete masonry units (CMUs)—while the nominal (macroscopic, geometrical)  s/v  is ~ 80 m −1 , the true  s/v  is expected to be substantially higher than this value. On the other hand, in real-world applications, a substantial fraction of concrete surfaces are protected by paints, sealants, or other coatings, which are frequently reapplied throughout the service life of a structure. These protective layers act as diffusion barriers, greatly reducing the surface area directly exposed to the atmosphere and thereby lowering the effective  s/v  available for CO 2  ingress. As a result, the actual rate and extent of carbonation in coated or painted concrete are significantly diminished compared to uncoated conditions 152 , 153 . Since precise data of the volume of concrete used in each component category, and its effective  s/v  is not readily available, once again, we assume a uniform distribution. Degree of hydration of OPC (DoH, 70–100%): a normal distribution was used ( µ  = 85%,  σ  = 5%). For reference, a typical OPC aged >28 days lies in this range 28 ,  29 – 30 . w/c  (mass ratio): the  w/c  was determined using a uniform distribution for each grade of concrete (Table  3 ):  C  ≤ 15 MPa ( µ  = 0.7,  σ  = 0.029),  C  = 16–23 MPa ( µ  = 0.6,  σ  = 0.029),  C  = 23–35 MPa ( µ  = 0.5,  σ  = 0.029) and  C  > 35 MPa ( µ  = 0.45,  σ  = 0.029). a/b  (mass ratio): the  a/b  was determined using a uniform distribution for each grade of concrete (Table  3 ):  C  ≤ 15 MPa ( µ  = 5,  σ  = 0.58),  C  = 16–23 MPa ( µ  = 3.5,  σ  = 0.29),  C  = 23–35 MPa ( µ  = 3,  σ  = 0.29) and  C  > 35 MPa ( µ  = 2.5,  σ  = 0.29). Cement clinker factor (C OPC , 0.6–1.0, mass ratio): a normal distribution was used ( µ  = 0.8,  σ  = 0.067). According to Andrew 72 , although U.S. clinker factors may be (were) as high as 0.90–0.95, the global average can be as low as 0.8, and is trending even lower, due to much lower clinker contents in Chinese and Indian cements, e.g., 0.60 and 0.79, respectively 72 . It is important to note that global cement production figures reported by the Global Carbon Project (GCP) 72 , 73  refer to OPC, including additives, such as gypsum and SCMs. SCM content (C SCM , 0–40, mass %) and CaO content of SCMs (0–40, mass %): a uniform distribution was used across both variables. Currently, Class C fly ash, Class F fly ash and blast furnace slag are the most widely used SCMs globally. Typical OPC replacement levels using these materials vary across regions based on prevalent standards in the range of 0–40 mass %, and depending on whether a binary or ternary formulation is used ( µ  = 20%,  σ  = 11.55%) 53 ,  54 ,  55 – 56 . These SCM materials vary substantially in their oxide composition, with CaO content ranging between (near) 0–40 mass % of CaO. Since CaO (and MgO) are dominant in carbonation, a range of CaO contents were considered to establish the carbonation potential ( µ  = 20%,  σ  = 11.55%). Here, the SCMs are assumed to have undergone 40% reaction after 28 days of aging 57 ,  58 ,  59 – 60 —a conservative estimate for more prolonged periods of aging.
